title: Lisa Tennant on chairing the Environment Agency: priorities, powers and public trust
label: 11 November 2026 · Pre‑appointment hearing
summary: Lisa Tennant, the Government’s preferred candidate for Chair of the Environment Agency, answered questions from two parliamentary committees about why she applied, how her experience in Scotland prepares her, and what she would prioritise. She emphasised three goals—keeping communities safe from floods and drought, cleaning water and air (including PFAS), and enabling sustainable growth—while recognising major operational challenges: restoring public trust, fixing inspections and enforcement, clearing permit backlogs, and guiding the EA through organisational change including a new water regulator.

Scottish Environment Protection Agency, Scotland's equivalent environmental regulator.

chapters.title: Why she applied and what she brings
chapters.takeaway: Tennant is motivated by a lifelong passion for nature and three years' experience leading SEPA after a cyber-attack; she commits to the full term and aims to learn the EA quickly.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Lisa, could you introduce yourself and say why you applied to be Chair of the Environment Agency?

turns.speaker: Lisa Tennant
turns.text: I grew up valuing nature, have run sustainable businesses, and currently chair SEPA and an NHS pension board. I applied because my SEPA role—stabilising the agency after a cyber-attack and preparing it for a merger—gives me experience I can bring to the larger EA.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: You left SEPA before your term ended. Do you commit to serving the full EA term if appointed?

turns.speaker: Lisa Tennant
turns.text: Yes, I commit to serving the full term.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: The EA is much bigger than SEPA. How will you handle the scale?

turns.speaker: Lisa Tennant
turns.text: I’d start by listening—travelling, meeting regional staff, mayors and partners—like my first 100 days at SEPA. There are similarities in issues, though England’s privatised water sector and different flood responsibilities are notable differences.

chapters.title: Three priorities: Safe, Clean, Grow
chapters.takeaway: Her board focus would be on safety from floods/droughts, cleaning air and water (including PFAS), and enabling sustainable growth, using outcomes-based metrics.

turns.speaker: Barry Gardiner
turns.text: What have parliamentary inquiries taught you about the EA, and what would be your top three priorities?

turns.speaker: Lisa Tennant
turns.text: Parliamentary scrutiny shows the need for partnership. My three priorities are 'safe' (floods and drought), 'clean' (water, air, pollutants like PFAS), and 'grow' (enable sustainable economic activity).

turns.speaker: Barry Gardiner
turns.text: How will you set sensible but stretching KPIs when the EA sometimes overdelivers on weak targets?

turns.speaker: Lisa Tennant
turns.text: I favour outcomes-based performance: check whether outputs lead to real environmental improvements. Use risk-based prioritisation to focus resources where they make the biggest difference.

turns.speaker: Sammy Wilson
turns.text: Should senior job specs require environmental experience?

turns.speaker: Lisa Tennant
turns.text: The right skills and regulatory mindset matter more than subject credentials. Strong regulators can come from other sectors, but they must be evidence-based and risk-aware.

chapters.title: Inspections, enforcement and rebuilding trust
chapters.takeaway: Tennant accepts public concerns about inspections and transparency, vows to review inspection standards, push for more unannounced checks, stronger enforcement and clearer public data.

turns.speaker: Sarah Gibson
turns.text: Campaigners say the EA is opaque and inconsistent: compliant operators feel penalised while flagrant offenders seem to get away. How will you fix that?

turns.speaker: Lisa Tennant
turns.text: I’d first learn how the EA currently inspects and enforces. In Scotland we published compliance data, doubled penalties for worst offenders, and publicly called out polluters to deter bad behaviour. Greater transparency and visible enforcement rebuild trust.

turns.speaker: Henry Tufnell
turns.text: The EA faces tens of thousands of FOIs and was served notices by the Information Commissioner. Will you change culture on openness?

turns.speaker: Lisa Tennant
turns.text: Yes—publish data early in an understandable form, make FOI handling more efficient and consider responsible use of AI to help with routine requests while keeping human checks.

turns.speaker: Sojan Joseph
turns.text: Some problems take years to act on—Hoads Wood ran on for four years. How would you handle multi-agency waste crime and earlier intervention?

turns.speaker: Lisa Tennant
turns.text: Early detection is vital. SEPA worked with police and HMRC on organised waste crime and used drones and satellite imagery. I’d review digital waste tracking, surveillance tools and joint enforcement arrangements to catch problems sooner.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: On high-profile incidents—like millions of plastic beads washing up—people say the EA was slow to respond. Do you see that as a failure?

turns.speaker: Lisa Tennant
turns.text: I can’t judge past cases without the facts. I will investigate and write to the Committee on specific examples, but I agree visibility and speed of local response must improve.

chapters.title: Operational pressures: staffing, permits and budgets
chapters.takeaway: She recognises recruitment, pay and permit backlogs as core problems; suggests better staff pathways, technology (including AI) to clear backlogs, and risk-based budget prioritisation.

turns.speaker: Terry Jermy
turns.text: The EA struggles to recruit and retain specialists, delaying permits. How would you improve that?

turns.speaker: Lisa Tennant
turns.text: Boards must understand workforce culture and retention risks. At SEPA we created non-management expert career paths, boosted training for new managers, ran apprenticeships and used staff surveys to target action.

turns.speaker: Ben Goldsborough
turns.text: On tight budgets, will you fight for funding or live within efficiency savings?

turns.speaker: Lisa Tennant
turns.text: Both: pursue efficiency—especially technology to cut duplication—and, where there is robust evidence of new risks, press Government for targeted funding as we did in Scotland for unregulated reservoirs.

turns.speaker: Terry Jermy
turns.text: Farmers need timely licences to make business decisions. Will you clear permit backlogs?

turns.speaker: Lisa Tennant
turns.text: I sympathise. There’s been progress—40% of the permitting backlog cleared—but digital solutions and AI pilots should be explored to speed complex cases while maintaining quality.

chapters.title: Organisational change and the regulatory landscape
chapters.takeaway: She has experience of large restructures and union engagement; will push for transparency during change, a live risk‑appetite approach, and close working with any new water regulator.

turns.speaker: Manuela Perteghella
turns.text: You managed big reforms in Scotland. How would you handle the EA’s restructuring under the Dan Corry proposals and a new water regulator?

turns.speaker: Lisa Tennant
turns.text: Major change needs clear delivery plans, milestones, early and honest staff engagement and visible board oversight. I set up an all-staff Q&A and published questions at SEPA; I’d do similar and work closely with unions.

turns.speaker: Manuela Perteghella
turns.text: Do you accept the EA must take more calculated risks to enable innovation?

turns.speaker: Lisa Tennant
turns.text: Yes—distinguish between core low-risk functions and areas where we can experiment. But make the risk appetite real through culture, processes and performance metrics that reward innovation.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: How will the EA relate to a new integrated water regulator?

turns.speaker: Lisa Tennant
turns.text: I’ll build relationships early. The EA should be a trusted partner in any new design; I’ll seek clarity on roles so responsibilities don’t overlap or fall between agencies.

chapters.title: Pollution, PFAS, air and climate resilience
chapters.takeaway: She places PFAS, industrial air pollution and climate adaptation high on the 'clean' and 'safe' agendas; supports nature-based solutions where evidence shows they work and wants the EA to prioritise flood/drought risk management.

turns.speaker: Cat Eccles
turns.text: PFAS monitoring is still limited and regulators are fragmented. How will you prioritise PFAS and coordinate work across agencies?

turns.speaker: Lisa Tennant
turns.text: PFAS sit under 'clean'. The EA should lead monitoring, research and enforcement while coordinating with other regulators. We must act on current evidence and not wait for perfect science.

turns.speaker: Jonathan Davies
turns.text: Air pollution causes many deaths. How would you raise the profile of air quality in the EA’s work?

turns.speaker: Lisa Tennant
turns.text: Air needs to be higher on the agenda. The EA should deepen partnership with local authorities on finer particle monitoring and use planning advice to prevent pollution.

turns.speaker: Adrian Ramsay
turns.text: Climate risks are growing faster than resources. What should the EA do about adaptation and nature-based solutions?

turns.speaker: Lisa Tennant
turns.text: Prioritise based on evidence: focus resources where flood and drought risks to life and property are greatest. I back nature-based solutions where they are proven, and want clearer investment and maintenance for natural infrastructure.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Any final personal reflections on the climate emergency?

turns.speaker: Lisa Tennant
turns.text: I think in terms of my children: volatility is increasing and we need long-term thinking. Nature recovery matters as much as climate mitigation, and both must be central to the EA’s mission.
